objectives.text: Perform addition, subtraction, multiplication and division with positive and negative integers.
Apply the correct order of operations (BIDMAS/BODMAS) to evaluate numerical expressions.
Use mental strategies for efficient calculation.
Identify and use factors, multiples and prime numbers in simple contexts.
Estimate answers by rounding before calculating.

diagnostic_items.stem: Estimate $49.7 \times 3.1$ by rounding each number to 1 significant figure.

theory_blocks.title: Why arithmetic fluency matters
theory_blocks.body:
Every topic in IGCSE Mathematics rests on confident number work. If you can add, subtract, multiply and divide quickly and accurately, you free up your attention for the new ideas in each unit.

Think of arithmetic as the alphabet of mathematics — you need it to read everything else.

theory_blocks.title: The four operations
theory_blocks.body:
The four basic operations are:

| Operation | Symbol | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Addition | $+$ | $7 + 5 = 12$ |
| Subtraction | $-$ | $12 - 5 = 7$ |
| Multiplication | $\times$ | $4 \times 6 = 24$ |
| Division | $\div$ | $24 \div 6 = 4$ |

[[green:Addition and multiplication are *commutative*: the order does not matter.]] For example, $3 + 8 = 8 + 3$ and $4 \times 7 = 7 \times 4$. Subtraction and division are **not** commutative.

theory_blocks.title: Negative numbers on the number line
theory_blocks.body:
Negative numbers sit to the left of zero on the number line. The further left, the smaller the value:

$$\cdots\;-3\;-2\;-1\;\;0\;\;1\;\;2\;\;3\;\cdots$$

[[red:$-5$ is *less than* $-2$ because it is further from zero in the negative direction.]]

theory_blocks.title: Adding and subtracting negative numbers
theory_blocks.body:
Rules for combining signs:

• $a + (+b) = a + b$ — adding a positive moves right.
• $a + (-b) = a - b$ — adding a negative moves left.
• $a - (+b) = a - b$ — subtracting a positive moves left.
• $a - (-b) = a + b$ — [[green:subtracting a negative moves right (two negatives make a positive).]]

**Example:** $(-3) - (-7) = -3 + 7 = 4$.

theory_blocks.title: Multiplying and dividing negative numbers
theory_blocks.body:
When multiplying or dividing:

| Signs | Result | Example |
|---|---|---|
| $(+) \times (+)$ | $+$ | $3 \times 4 = 12$ |
| $(-) \times (-)$ | $+$ | $(-3)\times(-4) = 12$ |
| $(+) \times (-)$ | $-$ | $3 \times (-4) = -12$ |
| $(-) \times (+)$ | $-$ | $(-3)\times 4 = -12$ |

[[green:Same signs → positive. Different signs → negative.]] The same rule applies to division.

theory_blocks.title: BIDMAS / BODMAS — order of operations
theory_blocks.body:
When an expression contains more than one operation, follow this order:

**B** — Brackets first
**I/O** — Indices (powers) / Orders
**D** — Division
**M** — Multiplication
**A** — Addition
**S** — Subtraction

[[red:Division and multiplication share the same priority — work left to right.]] The same applies to addition and subtraction.

**Example:** $3 + 4 \times 2 = 3 + 8 = 11$, **not** $14$.

theory_blocks.title: Applying BIDMAS to a multi-step expression
theory_blocks.body:
**Evaluate** $5 + 2 \times (8 - 3)^2 \div 10$.

1. **Brackets:** $8 - 3 = 5$
2. **Indices:** $5^2 = 25$
3. **Multiply/Divide left to right:** $2 \times 25 = 50$, then $50 \div 10 = 5$
4. **Add:** $5 + 5 = \mathbf{10}$

theory_blocks.title: Mental strategies for addition
theory_blocks.body:
**Bridging through 10 (or 100):** To add $47 + 36$, think $47 + 3 = 50$, then $50 + 33 = 83$.

**Compensation:** To add $99 + 56$, compute $100 + 56 = 156$, then subtract $1$ to get $155$.

Practise these shortcuts until they feel natural — they save time in exams.

theory_blocks.title: Mental strategies for multiplication
theory_blocks.body:
**Doubling and halving:** $16 \times 25 = 8 \times 50 = 4 \times 100 = 400$.

**Partitioning:** $13 \times 7 = 10 \times 7 + 3 \times 7 = 70 + 21 = 91$.

**Using near-facts:** $19 \times 6 = 20 \times 6 - 1 \times 6 = 120 - 6 = 114$.

theory_blocks.title: Factors, multiples and primes
theory_blocks.body:
• A **factor** of $n$ divides $n$ exactly. The factors of $12$ are $1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12$.
• A **multiple** of $n$ is $n$ times a positive integer. The first five multiples of $7$ are $7, 14, 21, 28, 35$.
• A **prime number** has exactly two factors: $1$ and itself. The first primes are $2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, \ldots$

[[red:$1$ is **not** a prime because it has only one factor.]]

theory_blocks.title: Finding all factors systematically
theory_blocks.body:
To list all factors of $36$, test divisors from $1$ upward and record both members of each pair:

$1 \times 36,\quad 2 \times 18,\quad 3 \times 12,\quad 4 \times 9,\quad 6 \times 6$

Stop when the pairs meet. Factors of $36$: $\{1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36\}$.

theory_blocks.title: Estimating by rounding
theory_blocks.body:
To estimate, round each number to one significant figure, then calculate:

**Example:** Estimate $387 \times 0.52$.

$387 \approx 400$, $0.52 \approx 0.5$

$400 \times 0.5 = 200$

[[green:An estimate lets you check whether your exact answer is reasonable.]]

theory_blocks.title: Key facts to remember
theory_blocks.body:
• Follow BIDMAS for the order of operations — brackets first, then indices, then multiplication/division (left to right), then addition/subtraction (left to right).
• Same signs multiply to positive; different signs multiply to negative.
• Subtracting a negative is the same as adding.
• A factor divides exactly; a multiple is a product.
• $1$ is not prime; $2$ is the only even prime.

objectives.text: Convert between fractions, decimals and percentages.
Find equivalent fractions and simplify fractions to their lowest terms.
Add and subtract fractions with different denominators.
Multiply and divide simple fractions.
Order fractions, decimals and percentages on a number line.

theory_blocks.title: Fractions as parts of a whole
theory_blocks.body:
A fraction $\tfrac{a}{b}$ means $a$ equal parts out of $b$. The top number (numerator) counts how many parts you have; the bottom number (denominator) tells you how many equal parts make the whole.

[[green:$\tfrac{3}{4}$ means 3 parts out of 4 equal pieces.]]

theory_blocks.title: Equivalent fractions
theory_blocks.body:
Two fractions are **equivalent** if they represent the same amount. You create an equivalent fraction by multiplying (or dividing) both the numerator and denominator by the same non-zero number:

$$\frac{2}{3} = \frac{2 \times 4}{3 \times 4} = \frac{8}{12}$$

[[red:You must do the same to top and bottom — otherwise the value changes.]]

theory_blocks.title: Simplifying fractions
theory_blocks.body:
To simplify a fraction, divide the numerator and denominator by their highest common factor (HCF):

$$\frac{12}{18} = \frac{12 \div 6}{18 \div 6} = \frac{2}{3}$$

A fraction is in its **lowest terms** when the HCF of the numerator and denominator is $1$.

theory_blocks.title: Converting fractions to decimals
theory_blocks.body:
Divide the numerator by the denominator:

$$\frac{3}{8} = 3 \div 8 = 0.375$$

Some fractions give recurring decimals: $\tfrac{1}{3} = 0.333\ldots = 0.\dot{3}$

theory_blocks.title: Converting decimals to fractions
theory_blocks.body:
Write the decimal as a fraction over a power of $10$, then simplify:

$$0.45 = \frac{45}{100} = \frac{9}{20}$$

theory_blocks.title: Converting between percentages, fractions and decimals
theory_blocks.body:
• **Fraction → percentage:** multiply by $100$: $\tfrac{3}{5} \times 100 = 60\%$
• **Percentage → fraction:** write over $100$, simplify: $35\% = \tfrac{35}{100} = \tfrac{7}{20}$
• **Decimal → percentage:** multiply by $100$: $0.72 \times 100 = 72\%$
• **Percentage → decimal:** divide by $100$: $45\% = 0.45$

theory_blocks.title: Adding and subtracting fractions
theory_blocks.body:
To add or subtract fractions, they must share a common denominator.

$$\frac{2}{5} + \frac{1}{3} = \frac{6}{15} + \frac{5}{15} = \frac{11}{15}$$

**Steps:**
1. Find the lowest common denominator (LCD): $\text{LCM}(5, 3) = 15$.
2. Convert each fraction.
3. Add (or subtract) the numerators.
4. Simplify if possible.

theory_blocks.title: Multiplying fractions
theory_blocks.body:
[[green:Multiply numerators together and denominators together:]]$$\frac{2}{3} \times \frac{4}{5} = \frac{2 \times 4}{3 \times 5} = \frac{8}{15}$$

You can cancel common factors before multiplying to keep numbers small:

$$\frac{3}{4} \times \frac{8}{9} = \frac{\cancel{3}^{1}}{\cancel{4}^{1}} \times \frac{\cancel{8}^{2}}{\cancel{9}^{3}} = \frac{2}{3}$$

theory_blocks.title: Dividing fractions
theory_blocks.body:
To divide by a fraction, [[green:multiply by its reciprocal (flip the second fraction):]]$$\frac{3}{4} \div \frac{2}{5} = \frac{3}{4} \times \frac{5}{2} = \frac{15}{8} = 1\tfrac{7}{8}$$

Remember: **K**eep the first fraction, **F**lip the second, **C**hange to multiplication (KFC).

theory_blocks.title: Ordering fractions, decimals and percentages
theory_blocks.body:
To compare a mixture of fractions, decimals and percentages, convert them all to the same form (decimals are usually easiest):

**Example:** Order $\tfrac{3}{8}$, $0.4$, $37\%$ from smallest to largest.

$\tfrac{3}{8} = 0.375$, $0.4 = 0.4$, $37\% = 0.37$

Order: $37\% < \tfrac{3}{8} < 0.4$

theory_blocks.title: Mixed numbers and improper fractions
theory_blocks.body:
An **improper fraction** has a numerator larger than its denominator: $\tfrac{7}{4}$.

A **mixed number** combines a whole number and a fraction: $1\tfrac{3}{4}$.

To convert: $\tfrac{7}{4} = 1$ remainder $3$, so $\tfrac{7}{4} = 1\tfrac{3}{4}$.

To go the other way: $2\tfrac{1}{3} = \tfrac{2 \times 3 + 1}{3} = \tfrac{7}{3}$.

objectives.text: Use letters to represent unknown values and write simple algebraic expressions.
Substitute numerical values into algebraic expressions and evaluate.
Collect like terms to simplify expressions.
Solve simple one-step and two-step linear equations.
Understand and use correct algebraic notation.

diagnostic_items.stem: Write an expression for 'five more than twice a number $n$'.

theory_blocks.title: What is algebra?
theory_blocks.body:
Algebra uses letters to stand for numbers we do not yet know (or that can vary). Instead of saying 'I think of a number, double it, and add three', we write $2n + 3$.

This compact language lets us describe relationships, set up equations, and solve problems.

theory_blocks.title: Algebraic notation conventions
theory_blocks.body:
In algebra:
• $3a$ means $3 \times a$ — we drop the multiplication sign.
• $ab$ means $a \times b$.
• $\tfrac{a}{b}$ means $a \div b$.
• $a^2$ means $a \times a$.
• [[red:Write $3a$, never $a3$.]] The number always goes before the letter.
• [[red:Write $a$ not $1a$; write $-b$ not $-1b$.]]

theory_blocks.title: Terms, expressions, equations
theory_blocks.body:
• A **term** is a single part of an expression: $5x$, $-3y^2$, $7$.
• An **expression** is a collection of terms with no equals sign: $2x + 3y - 1$.
• An **equation** has an equals sign and a value to find: $2x + 5 = 13$.
• A **coefficient** is the number in front of a letter: in $7m$, the coefficient is $7$.

theory_blocks.title: Substitution
theory_blocks.body:
To **substitute**, replace each letter with its given value and compute:

**Example:** Find $3a - 2b$ when $a = 5$, $b = 4$.

$3(5) - 2(4) = 15 - 8 = 7$

[[green:Use brackets around negative values to avoid sign errors: if $a = -2$, write $3(-2) = -6$.]]

theory_blocks.title: Like terms
theory_blocks.body:
**Like terms** have the same letter(s) raised to the same power:
• $5x$ and $-2x$ are like terms (both have $x$).
• $3x^2$ and $7x^2$ are like terms (both have $x^2$).
• [[red:$4x$ and $4x^2$ are **not** like terms — different powers.]]

theory_blocks.title: Collecting like terms
theory_blocks.body:
Add or subtract the coefficients of like terms:

$$4x + 3y - x + 5y = (4x - x) + (3y + 5y) = 3x + 8y$$

Different letters and constant numbers cannot be combined.

theory_blocks.title: Collecting like terms with negatives
theory_blocks.body:
**Simplify** $7a - 3b + 2a + b - 4$.

Group like terms: $(7a + 2a) + (-3b + b) + (-4) = 9a - 2b - 4$.

theory_blocks.title: Solving one-step equations
theory_blocks.body:
Use **inverse operations** to isolate the unknown:

• $x + 5 = 12$ → subtract $5$: $x = 7$
• $x - 3 = 10$ → add $3$: $x = 13$
• $4x = 20$ → divide by $4$: $x = 5$
• $\tfrac{x}{3} = 6$ → multiply by $3$: $x = 18$

[[green:Whatever you do to one side, you must do to the other.]]

theory_blocks.title: Solving two-step equations
theory_blocks.body:
**Example:** Solve $2x + 5 = 13$.

1. Subtract $5$: $2x = 8$
2. Divide by $2$: $x = 4$

**Check:** $2(4) + 5 = 13$ ✓

[[red:Always undo addition/subtraction first, then multiplication/division.]]

theory_blocks.title: Equation with the unknown on the right
theory_blocks.body:
**Solve** $15 = 3y - 6$.

1. Add $6$: $21 = 3y$
2. Divide by $3$: $y = 7$

It does not matter which side the unknown is on — apply the same method.

theory_blocks.title: Why checking matters
theory_blocks.body: After solving, substitute your answer back into the original equation to check it works. This takes a few seconds and catches sign errors and arithmetic mistakes — two of the most common reasons students lose marks.

theory_blocks.title: Key algebra rules
theory_blocks.body:
• A letter represents a number; $3a$ means $3 \times a$.
• Only like terms can be combined: $5x + 2x = 7x$, but $5x + 2y$ cannot simplify further.
• To solve an equation, use inverse operations to isolate the variable.
• Always check your solution by substituting back.

objectives.text: Understand the Cartesian coordinate system with $x$- and $y$-axes.
Plot and read coordinates in all four quadrants.
Identify the quadrant a point lies in from its coordinates.
Draw simple graphs from a table of values.
Read values from a graph, including between plotted points.

diagnostic_items.stem: What are the coordinates of the origin?
In which quadrant is the point $(-3, 2)$?
A point has coordinates $(4, -1)$. How far right of the $y$-axis is it?

theory_blocks.title: The coordinate plane as an address system
theory_blocks.body:
A coordinate system is like a street grid. The horizontal road ($x$-axis) and the vertical road ($y$-axis) cross at the **origin** $(0,0)$.

Every point's address is a pair of numbers $(x, y)$: go $x$ units along, then $y$ units up (or down if negative).

theory_blocks.title: The Cartesian plane
theory_blocks.body:
The **Cartesian plane** (named after René Descartes) has:
• A horizontal **$x$-axis** — positive to the right, negative to the left.
• A vertical **$y$-axis** — positive upward, negative downward.
• The **origin** where they meet: $(0, 0)$.

A point is written $(x, y)$: [[green:$x$ first (along), then $y$ (up).]]

theory_blocks.title: The four quadrants
theory_blocks.body:
The axes divide the plane into four **quadrants**, numbered anticlockwise from the top right:

| Quadrant | $x$ | $y$ | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1st (top right) | $+$ | $+$ | $(3, 2)$ |
| 2nd (top left) | $-$ | $+$ | $(-4, 1)$ |
| 3rd (bottom left) | $-$ | $-$ | $(-2, -5)$ |
| 4th (bottom right) | $+$ | $-$ | $(1, -3)$ |

Points on the axes are not in any quadrant.

theory_blocks.title: Plotting a point
theory_blocks.body:
To plot $(3, -2)$:
1. Start at the origin.
2. Move $3$ units to the right (positive $x$).
3. Move $2$ units down (negative $y$).
4. Mark the point with a cross or dot.

[[red:Always go along the $x$-axis first, then up/down.]] A helpful mnemonic: 'along the corridor, then up the stairs'.

theory_blocks.title: Reading coordinates from a grid
theory_blocks.body:
To read the coordinates of a plotted point:
1. Draw a vertical line from the point to the $x$-axis — this gives the $x$-coordinate.
2. Draw a horizontal line from the point to the $y$-axis — this gives the $y$-coordinate.
3. Write them as $(x, y)$.

theory_blocks.title: Plotting points in all four quadrants
theory_blocks.body:
**Plot and label these points:** $A(2, 3)$, $B(-4, 1)$, $C(-1, -3)$, $D(3, -2)$.

• $A$ is in the 1st quadrant (right 2, up 3).
• $B$ is in the 2nd quadrant (left 4, up 1).
• $C$ is in the 3rd quadrant (left 1, down 3).
• $D$ is in the 4th quadrant (right 3, down 2).

theory_blocks.title: Drawing a graph from a table of values
theory_blocks.body:
To draw the graph of $y = 2x - 1$:

1. **Make a table** of $x$ and $y$ values:

| $x$ | $-2$ | $-1$ | $0$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $y$ | $-5$ | $-3$ | $-1$ | $1$ | $3$ | $5$ |

2. **Plot** each pair $(x, y)$.
3. **Join** the points with a straight line (for a linear equation).
4. **Label** the line with its equation.

theory_blocks.title: What straight-line graphs look like
theory_blocks.body:
If the equation has no $x^2$ term (it is 'linear'), the graph is a straight line. Equations like $y = x + 3$, $y = -2x$, and $y = \tfrac{1}{2}x - 1$ all produce straight lines.

The number multiplying $x$ controls the steepness (gradient), and the constant shifts the line up or down.

theory_blocks.title: Reading values from a graph
theory_blocks.body:
To find $y$ when $x = 2$ from a graph:
1. Find $x = 2$ on the horizontal axis.
2. Draw a vertical line up to the graph.
3. From where it meets the graph, draw a horizontal line to the $y$-axis.
4. Read the $y$-value.

[[green:If the point falls between grid lines, give your best estimate.]]

theory_blocks.title: Key points on axes
theory_blocks.body:
• Every point on the $x$-axis has $y = 0$: e.g. $(5, 0)$, $(-3, 0)$.
• Every point on the $y$-axis has $x = 0$: e.g. $(0, 4)$, $(0, -2)$.
• The **origin** is the only point on both axes: $(0, 0)$.

theory_blocks.title: Coordinates checklist
theory_blocks.body:
• Coordinates are written $(x, y)$ — horizontal first, vertical second.
• The four quadrants are numbered anticlockwise from the top right.
• 'Along the corridor, up the stairs' reminds you of the plotting order.
• A linear equation produces a straight-line graph.
• Use a table of values to plot a graph systematically.

worked_examples.title: Identifying quadrants
worked_examples.statement: State the quadrant for each point: (a) $(5, -3)$ (b) $(-2, -4)$ (c) $(-1, 6)$.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Reversing $x$ and $y$ — writing the quadrant for $(y, x)$ instead.
worked_examples.exam_tip: Remember: $x$ is always the first number in the pair.

worked_examples.title: Completing a table of values
worked_examples.statement: Complete a table of values for $y = 3x + 2$ using $x = -1, 0, 1, 2$.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Writing $3(-1) = -3$ but then adding $2$ incorrectly to get $-5$.
worked_examples.exam_tip: Substitute carefully, especially with negative $x$ values.

worked_examples.title: Reading a graph
worked_examples.statement: From the graph of $y = x + 1$, read the value of $y$ when $x = 2.5$.

solution_steps.step: Go up to the line, then across to the $y$-axis: $y = 3.5$.

worked_examples.exam_tip: Use a ruler to draw your projection lines neatly.

guided_exercises.statement: Write the coordinates of a point that is $3$ units left and $5$ units up from the origin.

exercises.statement: Write the coordinates of these points: (a) $4$ right, $2$ up from origin (b) $1$ left, $3$ down (c) $5$ right, on the $x$-axis.
exercises.full_solution: (a) Right = positive $x$, up = positive $y$: $(4, 2)$. (b) Left = $-1$, down = $-3$: $(-1, -3)$. (c) On $x$-axis means $y = 0$: $(5, 0)$.
(a) Both positive → 1st. (b) $x<0, y>0$ → 2nd. (c) Both negative → 3rd. (d) $x>0, y<0$ → 4th.

exercises.statement: Complete a table for $y = 2x + 3$ with $x = -2, -1, 0, 1, 2$ and plot the graph.
exercises.full_solution: Substituting: $y = 2(-2)+3 = -1$, $y = 2(-1)+3 = 1$, $y = 2(0)+3 = 3$, $y = 2(1)+3 = 5$, $y = 2(2)+3 = 7$. Plot and join with a straight line.

exercises.statement: Write three different points that lie on the $x$-axis.
exercises.full_solution: Every point on the $x$-axis has $y$-coordinate equal to $0$.

exercises.statement: Plot the points $A(0, 4)$, $B(4, 0)$, $C(0, -2)$, $D(-3, 0)$ and describe what you notice.
exercises.answer: They all lie on the axes.
exercises.full_solution: $A$ and $C$ are on the $y$-axis ($x = 0$). $B$ and $D$ are on the $x$-axis ($y = 0$).

exercises.statement: Complete a table for $y = -x + 4$ with $x = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4$ and describe the graph.
exercises.answer: $y = 4, 3, 2, 1, 0$. Straight line sloping downward from left to right.
exercises.full_solution: When $x = 0$: $y = 4$. When $x = 4$: $y = 0$. The negative coefficient makes the line slope down.

exercises.statement: A graph shows the line $y = \tfrac{1}{2}x + 1$. Use the equation to find $y$ when $x = 5$.
Point $P$ has coordinates $(a, b)$ where $a > 0$ and $b < 0$. What quadrant is $P$ in? What quadrant is $(-a, -b)$ in?
exercises.answer: $P$ is in the 4th quadrant. $(-a, -b)$ is in the 2nd quadrant.
exercises.full_solution: $P$: positive $x$, negative $y$ → 4th. $(-a, -b)$: negative $x$, positive $y$ → 2nd (the opposite quadrant).

mcq.stem: What are the coordinates of the origin?

options.why_wrong: $(1, 1)$ is one unit from the origin in each direction.
This is one unit up on the $y$-axis.
$(x, y)$ is a general point, not a specific one.

mcq.explanation: The origin is where the axes cross, at $(0, 0)$.
A point is on the $y$-axis when its $x$-coordinate is $0$.

mcq.stem: The point $(3, -2)$ is plotted by going...

flashcards.back: The point $(0, 0)$ where the $x$-axis and $y$-axis cross.
$x$ (horizontal) comes first, $y$ (vertical) second. 'Along the corridor, then up the stairs.'

flashcards.front: Which quadrant has both coordinates negative?
flashcards.back: The 3rd quadrant (bottom left).

flashcards.front: How do you know a point is on the $x$-axis?
flashcards.back: Its $y$-coordinate is $0$.

flashcards.front: What type of graph does a linear equation produce?
flashcards.back: A straight line.

flashcards.front: Name the four quadrants in order.
flashcards.back: 1st (top right, $+,+$), 2nd (top left, $-,+$), 3rd (bottom left, $-,-$), 4th (bottom right, $+,-$).

misconceptions.description: Swapping the $x$- and $y$-coordinates when plotting or reading points.
misconceptions.remedy: Always write $x$ first (horizontal), then $y$ (vertical). Remember: 'along the corridor, up the stairs'.

common_mistakes.description: Joining plotted points with a curve when the equation is linear.
common_mistakes.correction: If there is no $x^2$ or higher power, use a ruler — the graph should be a straight line.

key_points: Coordinates are written $(x, y)$: horizontal first, then vertical.
The four quadrants are numbered anticlockwise from the top right.
Points on the axes have one coordinate equal to zero.
A linear equation gives a straight-line graph.
To draw a graph, make a table of values, plot the points, and join them.
summary.next_steps: You are ready for gradient and straight-line graphs.

objectives.text: Know the standard metric units for length, mass and capacity.
Convert between metric units using powers of 10.
Read values from scales accurately, including between marked divisions.
Perform calculations with time, including the 24-hour clock.
Choose appropriate units for a given measurement context.

diagnostic_items.stem: What time is $15{:}30$ on the 12-hour clock?

theory_blocks.title: Why measurement matters
theory_blocks.body:
Measurement turns the world into numbers we can compare, calculate with and communicate. You already measure every day — checking the time, weighing ingredients, reading a thermometer.

In IGCSE Mathematics, accurate measurement and unit conversion underpin geometry, data, and real-world problem solving.

theory_blocks.title: Metric units of length
theory_blocks.body:
| Unit | Symbol | Relative size |
|---|---|---|
| kilometre | km | $1\,\text{km} = 1000\,\text{m}$ |
| metre | m | base unit |
| centimetre | cm | $1\,\text{m} = 100\,\text{cm}$ |
| millimetre | mm | $1\,\text{cm} = 10\,\text{mm}$ |

[[green:The prefix tells you the factor: *kilo* = $1000$, *centi* = $\tfrac{1}{100}$, *milli* = $\tfrac{1}{1000}$.]]

theory_blocks.title: Metric units of mass and capacity
theory_blocks.body:
**Mass:** $1\,\text{kg} = 1000\,\text{g}$, $1\,\text{tonne} = 1000\,\text{kg}$

**Capacity (volume of liquid):** $1\,\text{litre} = 1000\,\text{ml}$, $1\,\text{cl} = 10\,\text{ml}$

[[red:Mass and weight are used interchangeably in everyday language, but scientifically they are different.]]

theory_blocks.title: Converting between metric units
theory_blocks.body:
To convert:
• **Larger → smaller:** [[green:multiply]] (more smaller units fit).
• **Smaller → larger:** [[red:divide]] (fewer bigger units needed).

**Examples:**
• $2.5\,\text{km} = 2.5 \times 1000 = 2500\,\text{m}$
• $350\,\text{g} = 350 \div 1000 = 0.35\,\text{kg}$
• $1.2\,\text{m} = 1.2 \times 100 = 120\,\text{cm}$

theory_blocks.title: Multi-step conversion
theory_blocks.body:
**Convert $4.7\,\text{km}$ to centimetres.**

$4.7\,\text{km} = 4.7 \times 1000\,\text{m} = 4700\,\text{m}$

$4700\,\text{m} = 4700 \times 100\,\text{cm} = 470\,000\,\text{cm}$

Or in one step: $\times 100\,000$.

theory_blocks.title: Reading a scale
theory_blocks.body:
To read a scale:
1. Identify what two neighbouring marked values are.
2. Count how many small divisions are between them.
3. Work out what each small division is worth: $\text{gap} \div \text{divisions}$.
4. Count from the lower marked value to the pointer.

**Example:** Marks at $20$ and $30$ with $5$ small divisions → each division = $2$.

theory_blocks.title: Time calculations
theory_blocks.body:
To find the time between $09{:}45$ and $13{:}20$:

1. From $09{:}45$ to $10{:}00$ = $15$ minutes.
2. From $10{:}00$ to $13{:}00$ = $3$ hours.
3. From $13{:}00$ to $13{:}20$ = $20$ minutes.
4. Total = $3$ hours $35$ minutes.

[[red:Do not subtract times like decimals. $13.20 - 9.45 \neq 3.75$, because there are $60$ minutes in an hour, not $100$.]]

theory_blocks.title: Choosing appropriate units
theory_blocks.body:
Choose the unit that gives a sensible number:

• Length of a pencil: cm (not km!)
• Distance between cities: km
• Mass of a person: kg
• Volume of a swimming pool: litres or m³
• Volume of a teaspoon: ml

Avoiding very large or very small numbers makes answers easier to understand.

theory_blocks.title: Conversion shortcuts
theory_blocks.body:
**Length:** mm $\xrightarrow{\times 10}$ cm $\xrightarrow{\times 100}$ m $\xrightarrow{\times 1000}$ km (reverse: divide)

**Mass:** g $\xrightarrow{\times 1000}$ kg $\xrightarrow{\times 1000}$ tonne

**Capacity:** ml $\xrightarrow{\times 1000}$ litre

**Time:** $60$ seconds = $1$ minute, $60$ minutes = $1$ hour, $24$ hours = $1$ day

worked_examples.title: Metric conversion

solution_steps.explanation: Move the decimal three places left.

worked_examples.exam_tip: Ask yourself: should the answer be bigger or smaller? Fewer litres than millilitres makes sense.

worked_examples.title: Time calculation
worked_examples.statement: A film starts at $19{:}50$ and lasts $1$ hour $45$ minutes. When does it end?
worked_examples.common_mistake: Writing $20{:}50 + 0{:}45 = 20{:}95$ and leaving it as that.
worked_examples.exam_tip: When minutes pass $60$, carry $1$ into the hours.

worked_examples.title: Reading a scale
worked_examples.statement: A weighing scale shows marks at $200\,\text{g}$ and $300\,\text{g}$ with $5$ small divisions between them. The pointer is on the $3$rd small division past $200$. What is the reading?

solution_steps.explanation: Divide the gap by the number of divisions.

worked_examples.common_mistake: Assuming each division is $10\,\text{g}$ without checking.
worked_examples.exam_tip: Always calculate what each division is worth before reading off.

exercises.statement: Convert: (a) $3.2\,\text{m}$ to cm (b) $750\,\text{g}$ to kg (c) $4500\,\text{ml}$ to litres.
Convert $5.6\,\text{km}$ to: (a) metres (b) centimetres.
Convert to 24-hour time: (a) $7{:}15\,\text{am}$ (b) $9{:}45\,\text{pm}$ (c) $12{:}30\,\text{am}$.
How long is it from $08{:}40$ to $11{:}15$?
Suggest the best metric unit for: (a) the height of a door (b) the mass of an apple (c) the capacity of a bath.
A thermometer has marks at $20°\text{C}$ and $30°\text{C}$ with $10$ small divisions between them. The mercury is at the $7$th division past $20$. What is the temperature?
A recipe needs $1.5\,\text{litres}$ of water. You have a $250\,\text{ml}$ measuring cup. How many full cups do you need?
A train departs at $14{:}47$ and arrives at $16{:}23$. How long is the journey?

mcq.stem: How many centimetres are in $2.4$ metres?
Which unit would you use to measure the mass of a car?

options.why_wrong: Too small — a car would be millions of grams.

mcq.explanation: A car has a mass of about $1000$–$2000\,\text{kg}$ ($1$–$2$ tonnes).

options.why_wrong: Forgets to add $12$ for pm times.

mcq.stem: A clock shows $23{:}50$. How many minutes until midnight?

flashcards.front: To convert pm time to 24-hour, you...
flashcards.back: Add $12$ to the hours. For example, $3{:}00\,\text{pm} = 15{:}00$.

flashcards.front: Larger to smaller units: do you multiply or divide?
flashcards.back: Multiply. More small units fit into the same amount.
$60$ minutes. (And $60$ seconds in $1$ minute.)

misconceptions.description: Not adding $12$ when converting pm times to 24-hour format.
misconceptions.remedy: For any pm time (except $12$ noon), add $12$: $2\text{pm} = 14{:}00$.

common_mistakes.description: Subtracting times as if they are decimals ($13.20 - 9.45 = 3.75$).
common_mistakes.correction: Use hours and minutes separately. There are $60$ minutes in an hour, not $100$.

common_mistakes.description: Multiplying when converting from small to large units.
common_mistakes.correction: Small → large means fewer units, so divide.

key_points: Kilo- means $1000$, centi- means $\tfrac{1}{100}$, milli- means $\tfrac{1}{1000}$.
Larger → smaller: multiply. Smaller → larger: divide.
For 24-hour time: add $12$ to pm hours.
When reading a scale, always work out what each small division is worth.
summary.next_steps: You are ready to tackle mensuration — area, perimeter, and volume.

objectives.text: Name and identify common 2D shapes and describe their properties.
Classify triangles by sides and angles.
Name and identify common 3D shapes and their features.
Identify lines of symmetry in 2D shapes.
Classify angles as acute, right, obtuse, reflex and straight.

diagnostic_items.stem: How many sides does a hexagon have?
What type of triangle has all three sides equal?
Name a 3D shape that has no flat faces.

theory_blocks.title: Shapes are everywhere
theory_blocks.body:
From floor tiles to football nets, from the cross-section of a bridge to the packaging of a box, geometry starts with recognising shapes and their properties.

Naming shapes accurately is the foundation for area, volume, symmetry, and transformation work in IGCSE.

theory_blocks.title: Polygons
theory_blocks.body:
A **polygon** is a closed 2D shape with straight sides.

| Name | Sides |
|---|---|
| Triangle | $3$ |
| Quadrilateral | $4$ |
| Pentagon | $5$ |
| Hexagon | $6$ |
| Heptagon | $7$ |
| Octagon | $8$ |
| Decagon | $10$ |

A **regular** polygon has all sides equal and all angles equal. Otherwise it is **irregular**.

theory_blocks.title: Types of triangle
theory_blocks.body:
**By sides:**
• **Equilateral** — all $3$ sides equal, all angles $60°$.
• **Isosceles** — $2$ sides equal, $2$ base angles equal.
• **Scalene** — no sides equal, no angles equal.

**By angles:**
• **Acute** — all angles less than $90°$.
• **Right-angled** — one angle is exactly $90°$.
• **Obtuse** — one angle greater than $90°$.

[[green:A triangle can be described by both classifications, e.g. 'right-angled isosceles'.]]

theory_blocks.title: Special quadrilaterals
theory_blocks.body:
| Shape | Key properties |
|---|---|
| Square | $4$ equal sides, $4$ right angles |
| Rectangle | Opposite sides equal, $4$ right angles |
| Parallelogram | Opposite sides parallel and equal |
| Rhombus | $4$ equal sides, opposite angles equal |
| Trapezium | Exactly one pair of parallel sides |
| Kite | Two pairs of adjacent sides equal |

[[red:A square is a special case of a rectangle (and also of a rhombus).]]

theory_blocks.title: Types of angle
theory_blocks.body:
| Type | Range | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Acute | $0° < \theta < 90°$ | $45°$ |
| Right | exactly $90°$ | corner of a page |
| Obtuse | $90° < \theta < 180°$ | $120°$ |
| Straight | exactly $180°$ | a straight line |
| Reflex | $180° < \theta < 360°$ | $270°$ |

theory_blocks.title: Lines of symmetry
theory_blocks.body:
A **line of symmetry** divides a shape into two halves that are mirror images of each other.

• Equilateral triangle: $3$ lines of symmetry.
• Square: $4$ lines of symmetry.
• Rectangle: $2$ lines of symmetry.
• Circle: infinitely many.
• Parallelogram (not a rectangle): $0$ lines of symmetry.

[[green:Fold the shape along the line — if both halves match exactly, it is a line of symmetry.]]

theory_blocks.title: Common 3D shapes
theory_blocks.body:
| Shape | Faces | Edges | Vertices |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cube | $6$ (all squares) | $12$ | $8$ |
| Cuboid | $6$ (rectangles) | $12$ | $8$ |
| Triangular prism | $5$ | $9$ | $6$ |
| Cylinder | $3$ ($2$ circles + $1$ curved) | $2$ | $0$ |
| Cone | $2$ ($1$ circle + $1$ curved) | $1$ | $1$ |
| Sphere | $1$ (curved) | $0$ | $0$ |
| Square-based pyramid | $5$ | $8$ | $5$ |

theory_blocks.title: Prisms and pyramids
theory_blocks.body:
A **prism** has a uniform cross-section along its length — slice it anywhere parallel to the end and you get the same shape. The name comes from the cross-section: a triangular prism has a triangle at each end, a hexagonal prism has a hexagon.

A **pyramid** has a base and triangular faces that meet at a point (apex). A square-based pyramid has a square base and $4$ triangular faces.

theory_blocks.title: Euler's formula for polyhedra
theory_blocks.body:
For any convex polyhedron (a 3D shape with flat faces):

$$V - E + F = 2$$

where $V$ = vertices, $E$ = edges, $F$ = faces.

**Check with a cube:** $8 - 12 + 6 = 2$ ✓

This can help you find a missing count.

theory_blocks.title: Recognising shapes in real life
theory_blocks.body:
Practice spotting shapes around you:
• A football is made of pentagons and hexagons.
• A can of soup is a cylinder.
• A road sign might be a triangle, hexagon, or octagon.
• Roof structures often contain triangular prisms.

The better you recognise shapes, the faster you can choose the right formula in an exam.

theory_blocks.title: Shape properties checklist
theory_blocks.body:
• A polygon is a closed shape with straight sides.
• Triangles are classified by sides (equilateral, isosceles, scalene) and angles (acute, right, obtuse).
• Special quadrilaterals have specific properties of sides, angles, and parallelism.
• Angles: acute ($<90°$), right ($90°$), obtuse ($90$–$180°$), reflex ($>180°$).
• $V - E + F = 2$ for any convex polyhedron.
• A line of symmetry produces a mirror image on each side.

worked_examples.title: Identifying a quadrilateral from properties
worked_examples.statement: A shape has $4$ sides. Two pairs of sides are parallel and all sides are equal in length, but the angles are not all $90°$. Name the shape.

solution_steps.step: All sides equal → could be a square or a rhombus.
Angles are not $90°$ → not a square.

solution_steps.explanation: A rhombus has equal sides but angles are not necessarily $90°$.

worked_examples.common_mistake: Saying 'parallelogram' — while true, 'rhombus' is more specific.
worked_examples.exam_tip: Always give the most specific name that fits all the properties.

worked_examples.title: Using Euler's formula
worked_examples.statement: A polyhedron has $5$ faces and $6$ vertices. How many edges does it have?
worked_examples.exam_tip: Check: does $6 - 9 + 5 = 2$? Yes. A triangular prism matches this.

worked_examples.title: Counting lines of symmetry
worked_examples.statement: How many lines of symmetry does a regular pentagon have?

solution_steps.step: A regular polygon with $n$ sides has $n$ lines of symmetry.
solution_steps.explanation: Each line goes from a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side.

solution_steps.step: A pentagon has $5$ sides → $5$ lines of symmetry.

worked_examples.common_mistake: Only finding $1$ or $2$ lines and stopping.
worked_examples.exam_tip: For a regular polygon, the number of lines of symmetry equals the number of sides.

guided_exercises.statement: A triangle has sides $5\,\text{cm}$, $5\,\text{cm}$ and $8\,\text{cm}$. Classify it by its sides.
How many faces does a triangular prism have?
hints: It has $2$ triangular ends and $3$ rectangular sides.

guided_exercises.statement: Is an angle of $195°$ acute, obtuse, or reflex?

exercises.statement: Name the polygon with: (a) $5$ sides (b) $8$ sides (c) $10$ sides.
Classify each triangle: (a) sides $3, 4, 5$, angles $37°, 53°, 90°$ (b) sides $6, 6, 6$ (c) sides $4, 7, 9$.
exercises.full_solution: (a) Has a $90°$ angle and no equal sides. (b) All sides equal. (c) No sides equal.

exercises.statement: Which quadrilateral has exactly one pair of parallel sides?
exercises.full_solution: A trapezium (US: trapezoid) has one pair of parallel sides. A parallelogram has two.

exercises.statement: State the number of lines of symmetry: (a) equilateral triangle (b) rectangle (c) parallelogram (d) regular hexagon.
exercises.full_solution: (a) $3$ (from each vertex to midpoint of opposite side). (b) $2$ (horizontal and vertical). (c) $0$ (a non-rectangular parallelogram has no mirror symmetry). (d) $6$ (a regular $n$-gon has $n$ lines).

exercises.statement: State the number of faces, edges and vertices of a square-based pyramid.
exercises.full_solution: $1$ square base + $4$ triangular faces = $5$ faces. Check: $5 - 8 + 5 = 2$ ✓

exercises.statement: A prism has a hexagonal cross-section. How many faces, edges and vertices does it have?
exercises.full_solution: $2$ hexagonal ends + $6$ rectangular sides = $8$ faces. $6 + 6 = 12$ vertices. $6 + 6 + 6 = 18$ edges. Check: $12 - 18 + 8 = 2$ ✓

exercises.statement: A polyhedron has $12$ edges and $8$ faces. Use Euler's formula to find the number of vertices.

mcq.stem: How many sides does an octagon have?
A triangle with two equal sides is called...

options.why_wrong: Equilateral has ALL three sides equal.
That classifies by angles, not sides.

mcq.explanation: Isosceles = two sides (and two angles) equal.
$250°$ is between $180°$ and $360°$, so it is reflex.

mcq.stem: Which 3D shape has $1$ curved face and $0$ edges?

options.why_wrong: A cube has $12$ edges and flat faces only.

mcq.explanation: A sphere has one curved surface, no edges and no vertices.

mcq.stem: How many lines of symmetry does a square have?

options.why_wrong: No 2D shape with $4$ sides has $8$ lines of symmetry.

mcq.explanation: $2$ through midpoints of opposite sides + $2$ through opposite corners = $4$.

flashcards.back: A closed 2D shape made of straight sides.

flashcards.front: Name the three types of triangle by sides.
flashcards.back: Equilateral (all equal), isosceles (two equal), scalene (none equal).
An angle greater than $180°$ but less than $360°$.
A 3D shape with a uniform cross-section along its length — its two ends are identical polygons.

flashcards.front: What is Euler's formula for polyhedra?
flashcards.back: $V - E + F = 2$, where $V$ = vertices, $E$ = edges, $F$ = faces.

flashcards.front: What is a line of symmetry?
flashcards.back: A line that divides a shape into two mirror-image halves.

misconceptions.description: Thinking a parallelogram always has lines of symmetry.
misconceptions.remedy: A generic parallelogram has NO lines of symmetry (only rotational symmetry). Rectangles and rhombuses are special cases with symmetry lines.

misconceptions.description: Confusing faces and edges on 3D shapes.
misconceptions.remedy: A face is a flat (or curved) surface. An edge is a line where two faces meet.

common_mistakes.correction: Check the properties: are all angles $90°$? Are opposite sides equal? Use the most specific name.

common_mistakes.description: Forgetting the curved face of a cylinder or cone when counting faces.
common_mistakes.correction: A cylinder has $3$ faces (including the curved surface); a cone has $2$.

key_points: A polygon is a closed 2D shape with straight sides; the name tells you how many.
Triangles: equilateral ($3$ equal), isosceles ($2$ equal), scalene (none equal).
Special quadrilaterals: square, rectangle, parallelogram, rhombus, trapezium, kite.
Angles: acute ($< 90°$), right ($90°$), obtuse ($90$–$180°$), reflex ($>180°$).
$V - E + F = 2$ for convex polyhedra.
summary.next_steps: You are ready for congruence, similarity, and angle properties.
